Even though the basic principles of chaetal formation are in all cases similar, the cellular machinery of chaetogenesis is highly plastic and allows the construction of the plethora of chaetal types (Tilic, et al., 2015a; Tilic et al., 2016; Tilic et al., 2017; Tilic et al., 2019b; Tilic et al., 2021a) (Fig. 2.4).

blocks.text: The major external body features of Annelida are described here, though some, such as branchiae, sensory organs, and reproductive organs, are dealt with in other sections.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The ‘head’ is composed of the prostomium, peristomium, and, in some cases, anterior segments (Fig. 2.2). The prostomium contains at least part of the brain, and often has eyes, antennae, and palps. Prostomia vary a great deal in shape from conical or semi-spherical, T-shaped structures, to elongate lobes that extend back along the body. In some cases, the prostomium may appear to be composed of two elements owing to a fissure line. In other taxa, the prostomium is transformed into a mass of palps or a radiolar crown and is hardly identifiable as a separate structure (Figs. 2.2c, h). In many cases the prostomium may be fused to the peristomium (Figs. 2.2a, i, k). In some cases, such as Maldanidae and Paraonidae, the joint structure is well separated from the rest of the body as a distinct head. In taxa such as Paraonidae, Phyllodocida, and Amphinomida, the only adult peristomial structure visible is the area immediately surrounding the mouth, and so the head is essentially prostomial, except where segments are incorporated into the head (most Phyllodocida, see below). In many taxa the peristomium is one (e.g. Arenicolidae, Cossura, Scalibregmatidae, Sabelliidae), or two (e.g. Eunicidae) complete rings separating the prostomium from the first segment (Figs. 2.2b, c, d, e, f, j). In taxa such as Acrocirridae and Spionidae, the peristomium may be difficult to see dorsally, but still appears to form a ring (Fig. 2.2d). Rouse and Fauchald (1997) scored many annelid groups as having a limited peristomium, as seen in Phyllodocida. While this is still accepted here for taxa such as Phyllodocida and Amphinomida, this interpretation has been revised for many other taxa following Rouse and Pleijel (2001).

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Head appendages include antennae, palps, peristomial cirri, and associated with one or more cephalized segments, anterior dorsal cirri. Antennae are always located on the prostomium. Up to three antennae may be present, including a pair of lateral antennae and one median antenna (Figs. 2.2a, b, i, k). Most common are simple, tapering or digitiform antennae (e.g. Amphinomidae, Hesionidae), though they may be articulated (e.g. Eunicidae), or consist of a basal ceratophore and a distal ceratostyle (e.g. Polynoidae). The lateral antennae may be located at or near the frontal edge of the prostomium (e.g. Hesionidae). In some cases, the lateral antennae are missing, leaving a single median antenna (e.g. Aphroditidae).
